title: Sliding Window Maximum
summary: You get a list of integers `nums` and a window size `k`. A window covering `k` consecutive items starts at the left end of `nums` and slides right one position at a time until its right edge reaches the last item. Return a list holding the largest value inside the window at each of its positions, from left to right.

examples.explanation: With k = 1, each window holds one item, which is its own maximum.

approaches.twist: Keep a deque of indexes whose values fall from front to back: pop smaller values off the back, expired ones off the front.
Push each value with its index onto a max-heap, and pop the top while its index has left the window.
approaches.note: Works, but every heap push and pop costs O(log n), so the pass is O(n log n). The target is O(n).

approaches.twist: For each window position, scan its k items and take the largest.
approaches.note: Works, but scanning k items for each of the n − k + 1 windows is O(n·k), up to about 2.5·10⁹ steps when k is n/2. The target is O(n).

signals.phrase: slides right one position at a time
signals.meaning: A window of fixed size: each step one item enters on the right and one leaves on the left. Update what you know instead of rescanning the window.
A value with a bigger value to its right in the window can never be the maximum again. Drop it, and the indexes left in a deque have falling values, so the front is the maximum.
k can be as large as n, so anything that rescans the window costs up to O(n·k). Each index should enter and leave your structure once.

constraintReading: len(nums) can reach 10⁵ and k can be as big as len(nums), so rescanning each window is O(n·k), about 2.5·10⁹ steps when k is half of n: too slow. A heap brings it to O(n log n). O(n) needs each index to be added and removed once, which a deque that pops from both ends gives. The deque holds at most k indexes and the answer n − k + 1 values: O(n) space.

hints.clarify: How many answers are there? One per window position: len(nums) − k + 1. Try [2, 7, 3, 1, 5] with k = 3 by hand: the windows are [2, 7, 3], [7, 3, 1] and [3, 1, 5], so the answer is [7, 7, 5]. Notice the 7 stays the maximum until it slides out.
hints.approach: Sliding window with a deque of indexes whose values fall from front to back. When a new value x arrives, pop every index off the back whose value is at most x: x is bigger and will stay in the window longer, so those values can never be the maximum again. Push x's index on the back. If the index at the front has slid out of the window, pop it off the front. Once the window is full, the front holds its maximum.
hints.whyNot: Taking `max` of every window rescans k items each time: O(n·k). A max-heap of (value, index) pairs works if you pop stale tops lazily, but each push and pop costs O(log n). Keeping a single running maximum fails as soon as that maximum slides out: you'd need the next largest without a rescan, which is what the deque keeps ready.

slots.setup: An empty `deque` of indexes, whose values fall from front to back, and an empty answer list.
slots.loop: Move the right end `r` across `nums` once; the window is `nums[r − k + 1 .. r]`.
slots.update: Pop indexes off the back while their values are at most `nums[r]`, then push `r`. If the front index is left of the window, pop it off the front.
slots.record: Once `r` reaches `k − 1`, the window is full: append the value at the front of the deque to the answer.
slots.return: Return the answer list, which holds one maximum per window position.

solution.explanation: Each index is pushed onto the deque once and popped at most once, from the back or the front, so all the pops together take O(n), and the pass is O(n) time even with a `while` inside the `for`. The deque holds at most k indexes and the answer n − k + 1 values: O(n) space. Only one index can expire per step, since the window moves one position, so a single `if` is enough at the front.

events.label: pop back
events.say: nums[{q[-1]}] = {nums[q[-1]]} is not bigger than {x}, which will stay in the window longer, so it can never be the maximum again: pop it off the back

events.label: push
events.say: Push index {r} ({x}) on the back. The values in the queue still fall from front to back

events.label: expire
events.say: Index {q[0]} is left of the window, which now starts at {l}: pop it off the front

events.label: maximum
events.say: The window nums[{l}..{r}] is full. Its maximum is at the front of the queue: nums[{q[0]}] = {nums[q[0]]}

events.label: return
events.say: The window reached the end. Return the maximums: {out}

predict.ask: Will the next value clear out the whole queue?
After this pop, will the new value pop the next index too?

related.relation: The same pop-the-smaller-values idea on a stack: there a warmer day pops colder ones and answers them; here the popped values are dropped and the front holds the answer.
Also a sliding window over a long input, but its size changes with the goal; here it's fixed at k and the hard part is the maximum inside it.
